Lesson 2 · Understand the problem

Where is the problem concentrated?

The repaired file gives us a trustworthy overall rate. The director now needs to know which parts of the chain create the largest service problem.

Baseline · weeks 1–8 · one average per store

Method in this decision: Distributions and comparisons

The decision brief

The chain cannot give every store the same amount of operational attention. The next decision is where to investigate first. We will turn the weekly records into one baseline average per store, examine the spread of those averages, and compare delivery-time groups. The result is a review shortlist and a clearer description of the workload that an alert program would face.

Follow the analysis
  1. Move from repeated weeks to store profiles
  2. Compare stores using their own group denominator
  3. Read time and store differences together
  4. Give the review team an identifiable shortlist
  5. Update the decision memo
  6. The bigger picture

Move from repeated weeks to store profiles

Start with the same repaired weeks 1–8. Average the eight weekly rates within each store. This produces 150 store profiles, each based on the same monitoring basket and number of weeks. The store table adds usual delivery time and urban location without creating extra observations.

The mean store rate is 12.74%; the median is 12.63%. The median puts half the stores on either side. The middle half of stores lies between 11.07% and 14.55%. These summaries answer complementary planning questions: total service burden, a typical store, and how widely the workload varies.

An average can conceal the stores that most often need help. A review queue should therefore retain the store-level rates and their operating context, rather than replacing every row with the chain-wide figure.

Compare stores using their own group denominator

Baseline service burden by usual delivery time
Delivery groupStoresMean rate (%)Stores above 10%Share above 10%
Long lead (4–5 days)7914.177898.73%
Short lead (2–3 days)7111.165273.24%

For each group, count stores whose baseline rate exceeds the 10% service target. Divide by the number of stores in that group. This denominator answers the manager’s question: how common is the problem among the stores that share this delivery pattern?

Long lead (4–5 days): 78 ÷ 79 × 100 = 98.73% above target

The mean rate measures severity; the share above target measures how broadly the target is missed. A group could have a few severe outliers or a widespread moderate problem. Showing both gives operations a better basis for allocating review time.

This chart answers a different question from the group table. It shows the chain’s weekly movement, while the table compares store averages over the full baseline. Both views use the same underlying observations. A store can have a high average in a generally difficult week, or a persistent problem across several weeks.

Use the delivery comparison to choose where to investigate the operating process. Ask store teams about replenishment schedules, promotions, and the products most often unavailable. The comparison describes where the burden sits; the alert pilot later measures what a particular action changes.

The shortlist contains store IDs that will remain recognizable in later data releases. Assign a reviewer to inspect the replenishment process at these stores and record what they learn. The table is a starting point for that conversation, not a complete description of every store’s needs.

The next lesson asks how much confidence to put in a new shelf audit based on a sample of stores. That will let the director weigh the cost of checking every location against the precision of a smaller audit.

Update the decision memo

The mean baseline rate is 12.74%, with the middle half of stores spanning 11.07%–14.55%. Retain group coverage and store IDs in the review list so the alert proposal responds to the actual distribution of service problems.

Make the call

To report the share of long-lead stores above target, which denominator belongs in the calculation?

Compare your reasoning

Use all long-lead stores. Dividing by all 150 stores answers how much of the whole chain belongs to that category, which is a different question.

The bigger picture

A business rule is experienced across a distribution. Describing a typical store is useful, but allocating scarce attention also requires knowing how many stores cross a threshold and how severe their problems are. The same logic guides staffing, inventory limits, and service priorities.

After your decision: open the known answer

All 150 store profiles are calculated from the same eight repaired weekly records per store. The group comparison introduces no new dataset and changes no stockout definition.
